# Playbook for ref_auction

When I'm shown a lot with an estimate and my personal valuation, I compare them directly. If my valuation is significantly below the estimate, I pass early rather than hoping to find value later—the estimate reflects the market's aggregate judgment.

When the standing bid is well below my valuation of the lot, I bid to compete. I calculate my profit margin (my value minus bid amount) and use it to decide how aggressively to push. High-margin lots deserve active bidding.

When deciding whether to raise on a lot, I check if the minimum raise would still leave me profitable. If bidding at the minimum raise gives me positive expected value, I bid rather than pass.

When I'm in the final round of a lot, I don't let perfect be the enemy of good. A bid that's below my valuation is worth making even if it's not the minimum profitable amount—I secure the value rather than risk losing it to another bidder.

When I have multiple lots remaining and budget constraints, I prioritize lots where I have the largest margin of safety (my value minus current bid). I don't chase marginal lots when high-value ones are still in play.

When other bidders have already won multiple lots, I don't let that alone motivate overpaying. I still bid on high-value lots for me, but I stay disciplined on the price.

I track my cumulative score as I go. Winning one lot at fair value puts me in a better position to evaluate later decisions—I know what profit target I'm aiming for.

I do not pass on high-value lots just because I want to conserve budget. Budget is a means to win valuable lots; the game rewards maximizing total value won minus total paid, not budget remaining.

# My Auction Playbook

When I see a lot's value to me is significantly above the estimate, I open with a modest bid well below my valuation to secure good margin while preserving budget for other lots.

When facing a raise from another bidder in round 2, I calculate my profit margin (value minus bid) and bid if the margin remains healthy, even if it means going to the minimum raise.

When a lot is worth far less to me than the estimate, I open with the minimum bid to test the market without committing capital, then pass in round 2 unless my valuation justifies staying in.

When I've already won lots early and have limited remaining budget, I recognize that opening with moderately high bids in middle lots burns capital I need for later competition. I should open lower and let other bidders establish the price first.

When facing the final lot, I calculate whether bidding at the minimum raise matches my valuation. If the minimum raise equals or exceeds my value for the lot, I pass rather than chase it.

When I notice my cumulative score from wins is low and competitors are far ahead, I should not bid aggressively on remaining lots just to stay competitive—I should focus on lots where my valuation significantly exceeds the likely winning price.

I will track my running total and remaining budget carefully across all five lots, not just focus on individual lot decisions in isolation.

2.text:
# Playbook for ref_auction

When I see a lot's value to me and the current standing bid, I calculate my net surplus (value minus bid) to assess whether the opportunity justifies my capital commitment at that moment.

When the standing bid is significantly below my valuation, I bid aggressively in round 1 to establish position and deter competition, using the minimum raise as a starting point rather than a ceiling.

When I'm in round 2 of a 2-round lot and I have substantial surplus value remaining (value minus current bid is more than half the current bid), I continue bidding to secure the lot.

When my remaining budget is low but a lot offers exceptional value, I calculate whether the absolute winning price I'd need to pay could exceed my valuation, and if so, I still bid because the expected value is positive.

When I win a lot, I must track my cumulative spending accurately across all lots to know my true remaining budget—I made an error treating a 30-unit starting budget incorrectly and this damaged my capital allocation.

When multiple lots remain and I've already committed significant capital, I preserve aggressive bidding for lots where my valuation is highest relative to the current bid (highest surplus potential).

When facing the final lot in a 2-round auction, if the surplus value (my valuation minus standing bid) is positive and meaningful, I bid to win it because there are no future opportunities to deploy my remaining budget.

Do not let the minimum raise constraint anchor me downward; it is a floor, not a guide for how much to bid. In early rounds, I can bid much higher than the minimum when my valuation is strong.
